Candlestick patterns

Source: vignettes/articles/analysis-patterns.Rmd
analysis-patterns.Rmd

A candlestick pattern is a shape made by one to five consecutive candles that traders read as a sign the price may turn or carry on, such as a hammer after a fall or three black crows after a rise. Every instrument inherits 61 methods that look for these shapes, one per pattern, from the CandlestickPatterns class. Each is a thin wrapper around one of TA-Lib’s pattern recognisers, called through the R talib package.

How the methods work

Every pattern method takes only the five range arguments of prices(), which are interval, from_date, to_date, days and adjusted. It fetches the candles, passes their open, high, low and close columns to TA-Lib, and returns the candles with one new column, named after the pattern, or NULL when UBI has no candles for the range.

The new column holds an integer for each candle, and the flowchart below shows how to read it.

flowchart LR
    V["Value in the<br/>pattern column"] --> A{"value"}
    A -->|"100"| B["Bullish match<br/>ending on this candle"]
    A -->|"-100"| C["Bearish match<br/>ending on this candle"]
    A -->|"0"| D["No match"]
    A -->|"200 or -200"| E["Hikkake confirmed<br/>candle_hikkake and<br/>candle_modified_hikkake"]
    A -->|"80 or -80"| F["A weaker match<br/>engulfing and harami"]

The value sits on the last candle of the pattern, so a three-candle pattern is marked on its third candle. Some patterns are bullish or bearish by definition and only ever produce one sign; others, such as the engulfing pattern, can go either way. candle_hikkake also reports 200 or -200 when a hikkake is later confirmed, which was seen over ten years of INFY candles on 2026-09-14, although its documentation describes only the common case. A check of the R port on 2026-10-07 found two more cases the documentation does not mention: candle_modified_hikkake reports 200 and -200 too, and candle_engulfing, candle_harami and candle_harami_cross also report 80 and -80, both in R and in Python, because both use TA-Lib’s own values.

Three details make the R values the same as Python’s. The talib package reports a match as 1 or -1 unless its option talib.normalize is FALSE, so each method sets that option for the call and restores it afterwards, which gives TA-Lib’s own 100 and -100. The talib package fills the first candles, which TA-Lib cannot judge, with NA, where Python fills them with 0, so the methods turn them into 0 and return an integer column. And the talib package’s candle settings, such as talib.BodyLong.N, default to TA-Lib’s own settings, which Python uses too; setting those options in an R session would change the R answers and not Python’s. On 2026-10-07 every pattern was run in Python and R on 400 fixture candles and on a 20,000-candle stress fixture made to reach rare patterns, and every signal matched on every row.

The full list

The table below lists all 61 methods in the order they appear in the code, in R/assets_analysis_candlestick_patterns.R as in the Python file. The “Pattern” column names the shape TA-Lib actually recognises, which is not always what the method name suggests: candle_side_by_side_white_lines, for example, calls CDLGAPSIDESIDEWHITE, the up or down gap side by side white lines.

Three column labels differ from their method names, because the methods were renamed to separate their words while the labels were kept so that code reading the data frames still works; the R port keeps the same three labels. The table below lists them.

Method Column label Why
candle_evening_doji_star candle_evening_dojistar The method was renamed from candle_evening_dojistar
candle_hanging_man candle_hangingman The method was renamed from candle_hangingman
candle_up_side_down_side_gap_three_methods candle_up_side_gap_three_methods The old label dropped “down_side”, and the mismatch was carried over

An example

The example below looks for engulfing patterns in a year of RELIANCE’s daily candles and counts the days a match was found. It was not run for this article, because it needs a live UBI; the column name comes from the code. All 61 methods ran without error over 270 INFY daily candles when the Python library ported them on 2026-09-14.

reliance <- Equity$new(exchange = "nse", symbol = "RELIANCE")
frame <- reliance$candle_engulfing(days = 365)

matches <- frame[frame$candle_engulfing != 0, ]
bullish <- matches[matches$candle_engulfing > 0, ]
bearish <- matches[matches$candle_engulfing < 0, ]
cat(nrow(bullish), "bullish and", nrow(bearish), "bearish engulfing days\n")

Each pattern method fetches the candles afresh, so scanning for many patterns sends one request per pattern. That is cheap against a local UBI, which caches candles in Redis, but if you want every pattern at once it is simpler to fetch the candles once with prices() and call the talib package’s functions yourself on the data frame, using the TA-Lib names in the table above, such as talib::CDLENGULFING. If you do, remember the two adjustments above: set options(talib.normalize = FALSE) to get 100 and -100, and expect NA rather than 0 in the first rows.
